passage: In their house in a small town near Ujjain, Shalini, fifteen, woke at six to fill the water drums, swept the courtyard, and made tea before school. Her brother Pradeep, sixteen, slept till seven. In the evening, she rolled rotis while he played cricket in the lane. Nobody said it was unfair. It was just how things were. But one evening, with her maths test the next day, Shalini sat with flour on her hands and felt tears prick her eyes. Her father noticed. "What happened, beti?" She said quietly, "Why is Pradeep never asked?" Papa was silent for a long moment. The next morning, he woke Pradeep at six. "Water drums. You and your sister, turn by turn."

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling as she rolled rotis before her test?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset at the unfairness, with tears pricking her eyes.

passage: In the village near Namchi, Tenzin, fifteen, was cooking dinner for the first time while his mother was at the monastery. His cousin Ankita watched from the doorway. Before touching anything, Tenzin washed his hands with soap at the tap outside. He cut the raw chicken on one board and the vegetables on another, then washed the knife. When the oil in the wok began to shimmer, he lowered the chicken in slowly, away from himself. Ankita's phone rang; she handed it to him. "Aunty wants you." Tenzin turned the gas off first, then took the call. "Why'd you switch it off?" Ankita asked. "Amma says the stove never stays alone. Not even for a minute."

passage: Ingrid, sixteen, was making dinner for her family in Stockholm while her parents worked late. Her friend Marek had come over to help. passage: I'm Tejas, and last winter I learned not to worship my phone's map. My friend Sharmila and I were riding a scooter from Mysuru to a waterfall. The map said, "Turn left for a shorter route." We turned back to the main road, asked at a tea stall, and got there by the highway.

grounding: A young traveller recalls following a map app onto an unsafe track and only then looking up and turning back.

passage:
Trek leader's note, Saturday.
Two of our group, Sarika and Chandrika, both twenty, left the main trail today to follow a "shortcut" shown on Sarika's phone map. The route led them onto a steep slope with loose scree, which the app shows as a path. Sarika kept looking at the screen, saying, "It says two hundred metres." Chandrika called me when the slope got dangerous. I reached them in fifteen minutes and guided them back along the ridge. Sarika was shaken and embarrassed. At dinner I reminded the group: the app helps, but look at the ground in front of you. From tomorrow, everyone stays on the marked trail.

qa.q: How far did the phone say the shortcut was?
qa.a: "It says two hundred metres."

qa.q: How did Sarika feel after being guided back?
qa.a: Sarika was shaken and embarrassed after following the screen onto a dangerous slope.

qa.q: What lesson did the trek leader give, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The app helps, but you must look at the ground in front of you, because the map showed a path where there was only loose scree.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that helped keep them safe?
qa.a: Chandrika noticed the slope getting dangerous and called the trek leader.

grounding: A trek leader's note shows a young traveller following a map app onto an unsafe slope until someone looks up and calls for help.

passage:
Dear Diary, Thursday.
Such a silly, scary evening. I was going to Yash's cousin's house for dinner in a part of Hyderabad I'd never been to. I walked with my phone in my hand, following the blue dot, not looking anywhere else. The app took me down a lane that got darker and emptier, past a closed factory. A dog started barking. Only then did I look up and realise there were no people at all. My stomach dropped.
I walked back to the main road, fast, and called Yash, who came to meet me at the petrol pump.
The app wasn't wrong exactly. I just stopped using my own eyes.
Zainab

qa.q: Where did Yash come to meet Zainab?
qa.a: At the petrol pump.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel when looking up in the empty lane?
qa.a: Zainab felt frightened, stomach dropping, on realising there were no people around.

qa.q: What did Zainab do right once the danger was noticed?
qa.a: Zainab went back to the busy main road and called Yash to meet at a public place.

qa.q: How might Yash feel getting the call?
qa.a: Yash was likely worried and quick to help, glad Zainab called instead of pushing on.

grounding: A diary shows a young traveller following a map app blindly into an empty, unsafe lane and only then looking up.

passage: I'm Baljeet, and at nineteen I thought I was a genius at cheap travel. Going home from Bengaluru to Amritsar for Diwali, I booked the cheapest combination: a night bus to Hyderabad, then a train with a forty-minute gap, then another bus. My friend Shalini said the gap was too tight. I laughed. The first bus reached Hyderabad two hours late. I missed the train. The next one with seats was the following evening. I spent the night on a station bench, clutching my bag, barely sleeping, scared of every stranger. I reached home a day late, exhausted, and missed the family puja. Cheap had cost me far more than money.

qa.q: How long was the gap between the bus and the train?
qa.a: A forty-minute gap.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel spending the night on the station bench?
qa.a: Baljeet felt scared and exhausted, barely sleeping and wary of every stranger.

qa.q: What would a wiser plan have looked like?
qa.a: Choosing a connection with more time between legs, or a more reliable route, weighing the hidden cost of a missed change.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel hearing about the missed train?
qa.a: Shalini might feel sorry for Baljeet and a little frustrated that the warning about the gap was laughed off.

grounding: A student recalls choosing the cheapest connections and losing a night, and some safety, to a missed change.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Monday.
Sahil, a second-year student, returned from his hometown thirty hours late. He had booked the cheapest option: an unreserved general coach and a connecting bus with only an hour's gap. The train was delayed four hours; he missed the bus and waited overnight at a highway dhaba. He told me he felt unsafe and didn't sleep. He also missed his lab exam this morning. His roommate Pranav had booked a reserved seat on a direct train for a little more and arrived on time. I have asked Sahil to meet his lab teacher today about the exam, and suggested that for long trips he compare reliability, not just price.

qa.q: How late did Sahil return?
qa.a: Thirty hours late.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel waiting at the highway dhaba?
qa.a: He felt unsafe and anxious, unable to sleep.

qa.q: What did the warden suggest, and why?
qa.a: To compare reliability, not just price, because the cheap plan cost Sahil a night, his safety and a lab exam.

qa.q: How does Pranav's trip compare?
qa.a: Pranav chose a reserved seat on a direct train and arrived on time without trouble.

grounding: A warden's note shows a student choosing the cheapest connection and losing a night, safety and an exam to a delay.

passage:
Dear Diary, Sunday night, 2 a.m.
Writing this at the Bhopal bus stand. I chose the cheapest route to Jagdish Chacha's wedding: a slow passenger train, then a local bus. The train was an hour late, the last bus had gone, and now I'm waiting till 5 a.m. under a flickering light. I've called Chacha, and he's asked a friend who lives nearby to come and sit with me, and I'm staying near the ticket counter where there are people. I'm tired and nervous.
I saved so little. And I've lost a night's sleep and half the wedding day.
Next time: the direct train, even if it costs more.
Hafsa

qa.q: Until what time is Hafsa waiting?
qa.a: Hafsa is waiting till 5 a.m. at the bus stand.

qa.q: How does Hafsa feel at the bus stand?
qa.a: Hafsa feels tired and nervous, waiting at night under a flickering light.

qa.q: What safe steps did Hafsa take after missing the bus?
qa.a: Hafsa called Chacha, who sent a nearby friend to sit with Hafsa, and stayed near the ticket counter where there were people.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Chacha feel getting the late-night call?
qa.a: Chacha was likely worried and quick to help, arranging for a friend to keep Hafsa company.

grounding: A student's diary shows the cheapest route leading to a missed connection and a lost night, and weighing reliability next time.

passage: You asked why I'm so fussy about travel. I'm Irfan, and I'll tell you about Lokesh's wedding in Jaipur. Two days before, I saved my tickets on my phone and emailed them to myself, kept a paper copy of my ID in my bag, and wrote three phone numbers in a notebook: Lokesh, his brother and the hotel. I reached the airport two hours early. At security, my phone died. No ticket, no contacts. I just handed over the paper copy and my ID. Then the flight was cancelled. I checked the next train on the station board and called the hotel from a borrowed phone, using my notebook. I reached the wedding four hours late, calm, instead of never.

qa.q: How early did Irfan reach the airport?
qa.a: Two hours early.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel when the phone died and the flight was cancelled?
qa.a: Irfan stayed calm, since the backups meant the problems were only inconveniences.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's preparations helped most?
qa.a: Keeping tickets and ID copies in two places, writing important numbers on paper and arriving early, which let Irfan switch plans quickly.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel when Irfan arrived four hours late?
qa.a: Lokesh would likely feel relieved and happy that Irfan made it despite the cancelled flight.

grounding: A young adult describes keeping tickets, ID copies and contacts in two places and having a backup plan, turning disruption into inconvenience.

passage: I work at the same desk as Ujjwal, and I've always teased him about his travel folder. Before every work trip, he prints his tickets, keeps a photocopy of his ID, and writes the hotel address and three phone numbers on a card. Last month we flew to Kolkata together for a client meeting. At the airport, Mahima, our manager, found her phone had been stolen. No boarding pass, no contacts. She looked panicked. Ujjwal calmly pulled out his folder: he had the booking reference for all three of us and the hotel's number. The airline reprinted her pass. I can't say what Ujjwal felt, but he looked completely steady. I've started my own folder.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal write on his card?
qa.a: The hotel address and three phone numbers.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal seem during the airport problem?
qa.a: He looked completely steady and calm, unbothered by the stolen phone.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal's preparation turn a crisis into an inconvenience?
qa.a: Keeping printed tickets, booking references and contacts in a folder meant the airline could reprint Mahima's pass quickly.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when she found her phone had been stolen?
qa.a: Mahima looked panicked, losing her boarding pass and contacts at once.

grounding: An observer describes a colleague whose paper backups of tickets and contacts turn a stolen phone into a small inconvenience.

passage:
Thursday. Wasim, twenty-five, had a job interview in Chennai on Monday. He booked the train for Sunday morning, not night, "in case anything goes wrong." He scanned his certificates and ID, emailed them to himself and kept printouts in a separate bag. He saved his friend Deepak's address in Chennai as a backup place to stay.
Sunday. The train was cancelled due to track repairs. Wasim felt his stomach drop, then remembered his plan. He took the afternoon bus instead.
Monday. He arrived at Deepak's flat at midnight, slept a few hours, and reached the interview office thirty minutes early, certificates in hand. The interviewer said, "Good, you're on time."

qa.q: Why was the train cancelled?
qa.a: Due to track repairs.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when the train was cancelled?
qa.a: He felt his stomach drop with worry, then calmer as he remembered his backup plan.

qa.q: Which parts of Wasim's preparation saved the interview?
qa.a: Travelling a day early, keeping documents in two places and having Deepak's flat as a backup place to stay.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel when Wasim arrives at midnight?
qa.a: Deepak might be sleepy but glad to help, since the backup plan was agreed in advance.

grounding: Shows over several days a young adult whose backups and early travel turn a cancelled train into an inconvenience.
